the-truncation-note-names-a-stale-limit.why:
OWNER DECISION 54's ONE FRAGILITY, EXERCISED. Her Arabic names the figure — «فُحِص أول ٢٠٠٠٠ سجل» — and the figure lives in the api. Raising the constant makes the sentence on screen FALSE with nothing else able to see it: no type connects an api constant to an i18n string, and the screen renders whatever the dictionary says. The lie is not cosmetic, because that note is the only thing telling a reader the scan was INCOMPLETE and there may be self-approval violations past the limit — a wrong figure makes a partial scan look like a measured one.
Kills `both truncation notes name the limit the scan actually uses` in `screen-copy.test.ts`, in BOTH languages at once, which is why the assertion checks each against its own rendering of the same constant — the Arabic in Arabic-Indic digits, the English in Western with a separator. A test checking one half would let the other go stale. The alternative design, interpolating the figure, was REFUSED: it renders through `formatNumber`, which keeps digits Western, and would silently overrule the owner's own numerals in a dictionary where Arabic-Indic digits in prose are the established convention (measured: 210 characters across 14 files).

an-undeclared-parenthetical-ships.why:
THE EXACT SHAPE THE DETECTOR COULD NOT SEE, PUT BACK — and this plant is the only proof the widening works, because it would have PASSED before it. `hardcoded-ui-english.py` reported 0 for this screen while `(truncated)` was on it, and the diagnosis was traced one pattern at a time rather than guessed: PROSE needs a capital and two words, TEMPLATE_PROSE needs backticks and two words, ONE_WORD_LABEL needs a colon, and BARE_TEXT_LINE's character class excludes the braces and quotes this line carries. A lowercase one-word parenthetical in a single-quoted JSX expression fell through all five.
Kills the hardcoded-English gate in `screen-copy.test.ts` with `undeclared 1`, naming `internal-controls|(partial)`. Note the word chosen is NOT one of the nine declared: declaring is keyed on the exact `screen|string` pair precisely so a NEW marker on an already-declared screen still fails flat, and this plant is what proves that rather than asserting it.

a-stale-declaration-is-left-behind.why:
THE DIRECTION A COUNT CANNOT SEE, which is the whole argument for a declared SET over a budget. A row declaring a string that does not occur sits there covering whatever lands next — so when one of the nine is finally translated, deleting its row is how the fix gets RECORDED, and forgetting to delete it silently re-opens the hole.
Planted, the script exits 1 with `STALE sla-dashboard|(sourced)` and the gate fails on the non-zero exit, which `screen-copy.test.ts` asserts separately from the count for exactly this reason. `(sourced)` is chosen as the near-miss of a real declared row (`(drafted)`), because the realistic mistake is editing a declaration to match a reworded string rather than inventing an unrelated one.
REPOINTED 2026-10-24 — THE THIRTEENTH TIME `plant --self-test` HAS CAUGHT A COMMITTED PLANT WHOSE EVIDENCE EXPIRED, and this time THE WORK RETIRED ITS PREMISE: owner decision 55 translated all nine parentheticals and the set was emptied in the same commit, so the row this anchored on is gone. Repointed rather than deleted, which is this repository's standing choice even when a premise retires.
AND IT IS REPOINTED AT A DIFFERENT MISTAKE FROM ITS BATCH-ELEVEN SIBLING, so the two are not one plant twice. This one EDITS an existing declared row to a variant that does not occur — the mistake somebody makes when a string is REWORDED and they update the declaration to match what they think it now says. `a-declared-row-outlives-its-reason` ADDS a row for a string that never occurred. Both surface as STALE; they are different ways of getting there, and the realistic one is this one, because a reword is the commonest reason to touch a declaration at all.

a-document-reads-the-local-name-again.why:
THE REGRESSION, ON THE DOCUMENT THE OWNER NAMED FIRST AND FOR HER REASON: a certificate of insurance exists to be RELIED UPON by a landlord, a lender or a regulator, so a name on it that is not the name on the company's licence is the worst instance of this defect in the product. The plant is byte-for-byte the shape `insurerName` itself had before item 3 — local first, then the catalogue, and the REGISTERED COMPANY ignored entirely — which is why it is the realistic regression rather than an invented one.
KILLS TWO TESTS IN `insurer-name-precedence.inventory.spec.ts`, BY DOCUMENT NAME: `each outward document resolves the insurer name through the ONE resolver` names the file and who reads it, and `NOTHING outside insurer-identity.ts spells the precedence itself` catches the second implementation. Two tests rather than one is a property of the design: *stopped calling the resolver* and *spelled the precedence itself* are different mistakes and a fix for one is not a fix for the other.
AND NO TEST OF THE DOCUMENT'S CONTENT CAN SEE IT, which is the whole reason this guard exists: nothing renders a wrong name today — no `Insurer` row on either database is linked to a registered company (dev 0 of 19, db-test 0 of 306) — so every rendered-output assertion stays green under this plant. The defect is latent until the first link, and a latent defect needs a guard over the SHAPE rather than over the output.
